raw_case_text:
A 43-year-old man from Jakarta presented with jaundice, preceded by nausea, vomiting, and abdominal pain for 7 days. The patient initially developed a flu-like syndrome for several days (fever and chills, headache, myalgia, and arthralgia). Over several days, he experienced passing tea-colored urine with decreased urine output. His medical story included asymptomatic chronic HBV infection for 11 years and never consumed anti-viral medication. The patient was treated as acute exacerbation of chronic HBV in another hospital for 2 days, but his symptoms were not resolved and was transferred to our hospital. He does not drink alcohol. Clinical examination on admission showed the patient was alert with profound jaundice. He had abdominal upper quadrant tenderness but no hepatosplenomegaly or ascites. Neurological examination was normal.
Baseline laboratory assessments and changes during hospitalization are shown in Table 1. Initial laboratory tests were notable for acute kidney injury (creatinine 13.18 mg/dL, ureum 327 mg/dL, eGFR 4.06 mL/min/1.73m2), elevated total bilirubin (36.06 mg/dL), indirect bilirubin (29.06 mg/dL), and liver transaminases, accompanied with anemia, thrombocytopenia, and hypoalbuminemia. Urinalysis revealed positive bilirubin and urobilinogen in urine, but no hemoglobin was detected. Polymerase chain reaction test was negative for Covid-19. HBV serological profile showed positive HBsAg, IgM anti-HBc, and anti-HBe, but negative HBeAg. HBV-DNA quantification could not be performed. He tested negative for hepatitis C, hepatitis D, and human immunodeficiency virus (HIV). Abdominal ultrasound showed normal liver size and parenchyma without signs of splenomegaly and ascites. Hepatic elastography revealed severe liver fibrosis (F3-F4) with median liver stiffness at 14.9 kPa.
The clinical scenario was initially interpreted as an acute exacerbation of chronic HBV. Treatment included telbivudine, cefoperazone, furosemide, ursodeoxycholic acid, and supportive management. On the second day of hospitalization, he developed altered consciousness with metabolic acidosis (pH 7.087, HCO3- 3.0 mmol/L) and oliguria (<200 mL/24 hours). Ammonia level was not measured. Further questioning to his wife revealed that his symptoms occurred 4 days after returning from a 1-year trip in Serui, Papua. At this time, rapid diagnostic test for malaria was ordered which showed positivity. Peripheral blood smear showed intraerythrocytic P. falciparum (63 parasites per 500 erythrocytes) with a high degree of parasitemia (12.6%) (Figure 1).
Diagnosis of severe malaria was made, and intravenous antimalarial artesunate with oral primaquine were administered. He was transferred to the intensive care unit, intubated, and started on continuous renal replacement therapy (CRRT) with continuous venovenous hemodiafiltration (CVVHDF) method, and after 4 sessions we observed an initial downtrend in ureum, creatinine, bilirubin, and liver enzymes level, accompanied with improvement in eGFR. However, over the following days his renal function continued to progressively decline, and the liver injury deteriorated. Eventually, he developed pulmonary edema, septic shock, multiorgan dysfunction and died on the seventh day of hospitalization despite cardiopulmonary resuscitation.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 43-year-old male presenting with profound jaundice, nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, and flu-like symptoms for seven days.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: A 43-year-old male presented with a 7-day history of profound jaundice preceded by fever, chills, headache, myalgia, arthralgia, nausea, vomiting, and abdominal pain. He experienced tea-colored urine and decreased urine output. He was initially treated for 2 days at another hospital for presumed acute exacerbation of chronic hepatitis B without improvement and was transferred for tertiary care. On hospital day 2, he developed altered consciousness, metabolic acidosis, and severe oliguria (<200 mL/24h).
subjective.past_medical_history: Asymptomatic chronic hepatitis B virus (HBV) infection for 11 years (treatment-naive). No alcohol consumption. Epidemiological history: Returned from a 1-year stay in Serui, Papua (malaria-endemic area), 4 days prior to symptom onset.
subjective.review_of_systems: Nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, dark tea-colored urine, oliguria; denies gross hematuria or respiratory symptoms.

objective.physical_examination: Admission: Alert, profound jaundice. Upper abdominal quadrant tenderness without hepatosplenomegaly or ascites. Neurological exam normal initially. Day 2: Altered consciousness, progressive oliguria, respiratory distress.
objective.routine_investigations: Admission: Severe acute kidney injury with creatinine 13.18 mg/dL, urea 327 mg/dL, eGFR 4.06 mL/min/1.73 m^2. Total bilirubin 36.06 mg/dL, indirect bilirubin 29.06 mg/dL, elevated AST and ALT, anemia, thrombocytopenia, hypoalbuminemia. Urinalysis: positive bilirubin and urobilinogen, negative for hemoglobin. Day 2 ABG: metabolic acidosis (pH 7.087, HCO3- 3.0 mmol/L). Viral serologies: HBsAg positive, IgM anti-HBc positive, anti-HBe positive, HBeAg negative; negative for anti-HCV, anti-HDV, and anti-HIV. SARS-CoV-2 PCR negative. Abdominal ultrasound showed normal liver size without ascites or splenomegaly. Hepatic elastography showed F3-F4 fibrosis (stiffness 14.9 kPa).

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Severe imported Plasmodium falciparum malaria with hyperparasitemia (12.6%), complicated by acute renal failure requiring renal replacement therapy, profound hepatic dysfunction, cerebral dysfunction, and multi-organ failure on a background of chronic hepatitis B. Rapid diagnostic test (RDT) for malaria was positive. Peripheral blood smear confirmed intraerythrocytic Plasmodium falciparum (63 parasites per 500 RBCs, 12.6% parasitemia). Serologies excluded acute HCV, HDV, and HIV coinfections.
Plan & Outcome: Initial treatment for presumed HBV flare (telbivudine, cefoperazone, furosemide, ursodeoxycholic acid) was transitioned upon malaria diagnosis to intravenous artesunate and oral primaquine. Transferred to ICU, intubated, and initiated on continuous venovenous hemodiafiltration (CVVHDF). Despite initial transient decline in azotemia and transaminases, multi-organ dysfunction progressed with refractory septic shock and pulmonary edema, leading to death on hospital day 7.
